note: The ONLY place two differently-spelled names may become one person. tools/compile_gazetteer.py keys the gazetteer on the whole normalized name, so nothing coalesces by accident; anything that should coalesce is declared here, with the judgement written out. Three rules the compiler enforces: a merge needs a `merge_rule`; the rule must name BOTH spellings verbatim, so it can be read back without the code; and same surname with different initials NEVER merges, rule or no rule — the 1835 letter lists are full of families and an initial is often the only thing separating two of them. AN UNREAD INITIAL IS A POSITION, NOT AN ABSENCE (T-0397). Where a printing sets `[?]` for a forename initial the parse records it as UNREAD, in the slot it was printed in, and UNREAD equals no letter — so `[?]. M. Fish` reads `[?] M.` against `E. M. Fish`'s `E. M.` and the two still refuse. Before T-0397 the marker was DELETED, which handed the initial to whatever letter stood behind it: `[?]rah Fowler` read as `R.`, `[?]nn M. Gooding` as `N. M.`, and `[?]. M. Fish` as `M.` in first position. All seventeen `[?]` refusals below were STATED on such a reading, so this file asserted letters no printing carried. The refusals themselves did not move — 177 merges and 29 refusals before and after — only their stated grounds, which are now what the page says. WHETHER an unread initial may be joined to a read one at the same entry of the same list is NOT settled here: it is a change to the identity POLICY and it is the owner's, and T-0392 carries the question and the eighteen duplicates it would resolve.

passes.what: The list of letters remaining in the Post Office at Chicago on 1 July 1834, which the Democrat printed three times — 1834-07-02 (page 3 column 2, the cut printing that kept one sub-column only: 150 names), 1834-07-09 (page 1 column 2: 298) and 1834-07-16 (page 1 column 2: 298, and its reading pass declares it the best witness of the three). Three witnesses to ONE list, read independently, each cut differently by the segmenter.
passes.method: The three readings are aligned BY POSITION — the list is one ordered sequence and every printing carries it in the same order, so the n-th entry of one printing is the n-th entry of the others. A pair is a merge candidate only where the alignment puts the two readings at the same entry; the difference between them is then either the transcriber's bracketing (`difference: markup`) or a recognition-class difference in one printing's type (`difference: recognition`). Nothing is merged on resemblance alone, and no claim's `normalized` reading was edited to make a merge easier.
passes.canonical: The reading kept is a positive one before an uncertain one — `[?]` and an `[uncertain: ...]` wrapper are readings that could NOT be made — then the printing declared the best witness, then the least bracketing. A bracketed letter is a letter the transcriber read through and supplied, so it is a correction and not a defect, which is why `John [H]. Kin[g]` outranks `John H. Kiny` rather than the other way about.
passes.not_this_list: Two OTHER post offices' returns are printed in the same three issues and are excluded from the alignment: Plainfield (1834-07-02 c039, 1834-07-09 c014) and Juliet (1834-07-16 c013). Reading them as one list is exactly the error the alignment makes otherwise — before they were excluded it proposed merging `William Wood` of Plainfield into `William Webster` of Juliet.
passes.open_question: T-0348. Seventeen of the refusals are an initial one printing could not read against the same initial another printing prints whole, which is not the family case the rule was written for; eleven are two READ initials that disagree, which is exactly that case; one is an initial present in one printing and absent in the other. The mechanism cannot tell them apart, so all twenty-nine are refused and the ruling is the owner's.

passes.what: A repair to the NAME PARSE the refusals below are stated on, not to the policy. `initials()` deleted the `[?]` marker before splitting a forename, so an unread initial either vanished or was replaced by the next letter of the same word.
passes.method: The marker becomes a sentinel that survives the bracket strip and stays welded to the word it opens, so `[?]rah` is ONE forename whose initial is unread, and `[?]. M. Fish` keeps M in second position. UNREAD is a value in the initials tuple and is equal to no letter.

The policy question itself is open and is T-0392's.

passes.what: THE OCR'S TURKISH ALPHABET, AND THE ONE MERGE IT COST. Seven readings in the corpus carried a letter no compositor in 1835 Chicago had in his case: the dotless i (U+0131), the capital I with a dot above it (U+0130) and the capital G under a breve (U+011E) — three letters Turkish has and the Latin alphabet this project transcribes does not. They are the signature of an OCR run whose language model was Turkish, not of anything the Democrat set, and tools/repair_ocr_turkish_alphabet.py maps each back to its base letter in every READING while leaving every `quote` — and every claim `notes` that quotes the artefact to explain a correction — character for character as it was. The letters are named here rather than typed, because that pass's gate refuses one anywhere in data/.
passes.method: The substitution is demonstrated and not inferred from resemblance. The 1834-08-06 reading of JOHN H. KINZIE, whose I carried a dot above it, becomes the name every other impression in the corpus sets; the 1833-11-26 reading of JOHN WRIGHT, whose G carried a breve, becomes WRIGHT, which that claim's own notes already called a spurious breve and a recognition artefact; and the dotless-i reading of Benjamin Swena becomes the Benjamin Swena that T-0299 had ALREADY ruled the same entry of the same list, aligned by position across three printings. No word is repaired, only a character: the dotless-i reading of William Bandle becomes `Willinm Bandle` and stops there, still refused against Fergus 1843's `Willis` because two full forenames that differ do not merge.
passes.result: ONE MERGE RETIRED, and it is the Swena one that stood among this file's 1834-07-09 entries: the two spellings are now ONE STRING, so the gazetteer coalesces them on its own key and a declared merge of a name into itself is not a judgement at all. 177 declared person merges become 176. Nothing else merged or unmerged, and no person count moved: what changed is that three names the town holds are spelled with letters a hand could have written.

firm_note: The firms' half of the same policy (T-0304). A business is keyed on its whole normalized name too, so nothing coalesces by accident; anything that should coalesce is declared in `firm_merges`, with the judgement written out. The rules the compiler enforces are the person ones with ONE deliberate difference. A merge needs a `merge_rule`; the rule must name BOTH spellings verbatim; and the two styles must carry the same set of PARTNER SURNAMES, with or without a rule, because a partnership is its partners and a changed one is a different house. What does NOT carry over from the person policy is the initial: for a person a differing forename initial is fatal, because the letter lists are full of families, but a '& Co.' style routinely elides or misprints the forename it trades under — the Wilson house below is printed 'J. L.', 'Jno. L.', 'Jno. S.', 'Jno.' and bare 'L.' across eleven months — so the same rule applied to firms would refuse every merge a firm actually needs. A second guard replaces it and is about the ground rather than the name: two styles the papers put in different STREETS never merge, because a firm that moved is documented by a removal notice, and a removal notice is a claim. ONE LOOSENING, and it is T-0340's (2026-08-29). A style that names NO partner at all — a heading whose signature went with the woven half of the column, which is the commonest thing a segmenter does to an advertisement — cannot contradict one that does, because an empty set is not a different partnership; it is a printing that did not say. So the guard reads: two styles that each NAME partners must name the same ones, and where one names none the guard has nothing to compare and the merge rests entirely on its stated rule. The escape is not free. A style counts as naming none only where `firm_sign_names` below declares it a SIGN-NAME — the shop's own name over its door — and the compiler refuses that declaration for any house a claim ever signed with a proprietor, refuses one whose two halves do not put the style back together verbatim, and refuses one for a business no claim carries. `firm_sign_names` is also what lets a style say both things at once: 'Russell & Clift, Chicago Book and Stationary Store' is partners AND sign run together, and without the declaration `firm_style` reads 'Book' and 'Store' as two more partners, because the heuristic it runs on is that partners are capitalised and trades are not — and a sign-name is a capitalised trade.

firm_merges.merge_rule: 'Jno. L. Wilson & Co.' is 'J. L. Wilson & Co.' with the forename set as the abbreviation this corpus uses for John rather than as an initial. The woolen-yarn notice of 1834-10-15 sets “JNO. 'L. WILBON & Co.” over “Dearborn ot.”, and the standing dry-goods advertisement running either side of it — 1834-09-17 and 1834-11-12 — puts the same house in Dearborn street, next door to the city boot, shoe and leather store. Same surname, same middle initial, same street, overlapping weeks. Merged INTO the 'J. L.' spelling because that record carries the relative placement and the full stock; the direction is which record can be placed, not which spelling is truer.

'Jno. S. Wilson & Co' is 'J. L. Wilson & Co.' with the middle initial misread. The claim rests on the transcription contradicting ITSELF: one stone-ware notice is printed twice and the same character reads “JNO. S. WILSON & CO.” on 1834-11-05 and “JNO, 8. WILSON & CO.” — a digit — on 1834-12-03, so that letter is not legible in this advertisement, while the readings that ARE legible in the same weeks and the same Dearborn-street give L. The trade string is the fixture's own, word for word: dry goods, groceries, hardware and crockery. This is an OCR variant of one house, not a second Wilson.

'Jno. Wilson & Co.' is 'J. L. Wilson & Co.' with the middle initial dropped, which is what the American does with the house all summer: the consignment advertisement of 1835-06-20 and 1835-07-18 carries one copy date, “Chicago, June 12, 1835”, and sells window glass, window sash, dry goods, groceries and hardware — the Democrat house's own stock, which listed window glass and wrought-iron hinges from Dearborn street the autumn before. Chicago's papers of 1834-35 name no second Wilson house anywhere in this corpus, so there is nothing the shortened style could be confused with. The American gives no street, so the merge takes Dearborn street from the record that does and invents nothing.

'L. Wilson & Co.' is 'J. L. NOTE WHAT THE MERGE DOES TO THE PLACEMENT, AND WHAT IT NO LONGER DECIDES (T-0403): `placement_rank` prefers a corner to a relative offset and is blind to date, so this merge hands the surviving record the 1834 corner although the 1835 colophon is the later reading. That choice is PROVISIONAL and always was — the merge keeps every printing's reading, so the ordering can be declared afterwards — and it is declared, in `anchor_changes` for business_chicago_democrat_printing_office, which runs after this pass and puts the office over Jones & King's hardware store in the scene.

E. K. HUBBARD.' — and the Democrat reprints it at 1835-07-01 c017, 1835-07-08 c005 and 1835-07-29 c011 with the line breaks in different places and not one word changed. 'S. Abell, attorney and counsellor' and 'Abell' are one law office's standing card in the two papers, and the bare surname is only the forename lost off a damaged line. The Democrat of 1835-06-24 c006 survives as every OTHER line of itself — '[…] ABELL, [ATTORNEY &] COUNSELLOR AT LA[W,] [CHIC]AGO, ILLINOIS, [attending] strictly to his profession[, he] hopes [for a share of public pa]tronage. Law Conveyancing [done with ac]curacy and despatch.' — and the American of 1835-08-01 c003 sets the same six clauses in the same order with the name whole: 'S. ABELL, [AT]TORNEY AND COUNSELLOR AT [LAW]. [CH]ICAGO, ILLINO[IS]. [B]y [devoting himself e]ntir[e]ly to his profession [he solicits a share of public] patronage. Land Conveyanc[ing done w]ith [ne]a[t]n[e]s[s] and de[s]patch.' Conveyancing named as a line of business is what makes the pair unmistakable: the American's own claim note records it as the FIRST of the town's law cards to advertise it, so the Democrat's card six weeks earlier is not a second lawyer doing the same rare thing. This corpus names no other Abell. Merged INTO the styled record because it is the one printing that sets the forename initial at all, and the Dearborn Street reading the Democrat holds survives the merge under `placement_rank` — nothing is placed here that the damaged line did not already say, and its missing preposition stays missing.

firm_merges.from: J. H. Collins & J. D. Caton

The card is copy-dated Jan. 20, 1834 in both records — 1834-01-28 c007 in the surviving one, 1834-02-04 c009 in the other — and both printings put the office next door east of Brewster, Hogan & Co. in South Water street (1834-02-11 c005 sets it 'door east. of Brewster, Hogan & C:'). Same two partner surnames, same street, same anchor, same copy date, and the two runs interleave week by week through the spring of 1834. Merged INTO 'Collins & Caton' because that record is the one that can be placed for the whole period: it carries the later card that moves the office two doors east of the Baptist Church, up stairs, South Water-street (1834-06-04 c003 through 1835-05-20 c014), which the initialled record never prints.

'Giles Spring' is 'G. Spring' with the forename printed whole, and one card ties the two forms together: BOTH records carry the copy date Dec. 3, 1834 — 'G. Spring' at 1834-12-03 among its copy dates, 'Giles Spring' at 1834-11-12 c008 and 1834-11-26 c009 — and both set the office 'second door west from the corner of Franklin and South Water streets'. The removal is printed on both sides too: 'Giles Spring' takes the office first door north from the Tremont House on Dearborn-street at 1835-05-20 c022, and 'G. Spring' prints the same removal at 1835-08-05 c019. One attorney, one office, one move. Merged INTO 'G. Spring' because that record holds ten printings against three and both anchors across the whole run.

'John S. C. Hogan' is 'J. S. C. Hogan' with the forename printed whole, and the printing that ties the two forms is the Brewster, Hogan & Co. dissolution — set at 1834-03-04 c010 and again at 1834-06-11 c002, where the record 'John S. C. Hogan' comes from. Its tail reads 'The business will be continued at the old stand, by Jno. S. C. Hogan, where he intends keeping on hand a general assortment as heretofore', the March printing puts the dissolved firm's stand in South Water Street, and from 25 March 1834 (c010) 'J. S. C. HOGAN' advertises on his own account in that street, with 'general assortment' among the goods, one door from the Post Office he kept (1834-08-13 c017). Same man, same trade, same street, three weeks apart. Merged INTO 'J. S. C. Hogan': that is the record that can be placed — the succession notice states no address at all, and the merge does not give it one, since the Post Office anchor it inherits is the store's own printing and not the notice's.

'J. Bates, Jr.' and 'John Bates, Jr.' are one advertiser, and the register holds them apart only because a third notice prints the forename whole. The same advertisement runs on both sides of the split: 'For Sale, 12 KEGS BLASTING POWDER … 16 heavy Steel Pointed CROWBARS … Enquire of J. BATES, Jr.' at 1833-11-26 c007, and 'For Sale, [7] KEGS BLASTING POWDER, and 16 heavy Steel Pointed CROWBARS. Enquire of J. BATES, Jr., at P. Office' at 1834-03-04 c024 — the same sixteen crowbars, the kegs down from twelve to seven, and BOTH signed with the initial. The Post Office anchor is on both records as well (1833-11-26 c021 'Enquire of J. Bates, Jr., at the P[ost] O[ffice]'). Merged INTO 'John Bates, Jr.' because that record can be placed — its live reading is the Post Office relative — and because its trade is the one the papers actually name, the auctioneer's licence of Jan. 25 (1834-06-11 c015); the 'merchant' of the other record is the extractor's and its own claim says no trade is stated.

One printing names both styles, which is as direct as this evidence gets: the dissolution notice filed under 'J. Wellmaker & Co.' at 1834-03-25 c004 reads 'the co-partnership existing between the subscriber and William Adams, under the firm of John Wellmaker [& Co.]', and 1834-04-08 c013 is that same notice reprinted, copy-dated March 4, 1834, 'under the firm of John Wellmaker & Co.' and signed JOHN WELLMAKER. So 'John Wellmaker & Co.' is the firm style the notice sets out and 'J. Wellmaker & Co.' is how the same man signed the closing notice of 4 March (1834-03-04 c011, 'J. WELLMAKER & Co.'). Same surname, same dissolution, one week's remove. Merged INTO 'J. Wellmaker & Co.' because neither style can be placed — no printing gives this house a street — and that record holds both March notices and both partners, John Wellmaker and William Adams, where the other names only the subscriber. Both sides are contradicted notices and the merge keeps both contradictions, so the house stays out of the 1835 town.

'D. Elston & Co.' is 'Daniel Elston & [Co.]' with the forename abbreviated, and the two are one works. They are printed in the SAME issue on 18 February 1834 — the smoke-house notice at c002 signed 'D. Elston & [Co.]' and the Chicago Soap and Candle Manufactory at c009 begging leave to inform the public as 'Messrs. DANIEL ELSTON & CO.' — and the smoke-house notice's copy date, Chicago, Feb. 15, 1834, stands on both records. The goods are the two ends of one raw-material stream and the corpus already reads them that way: cash paid for tallow and house ashes against hams, flitches of bacon and mess pork, from the same hogs. Merged INTO 'Daniel Elston & [Co.]' — neither style can be placed, so the direction is which record holds more of the house: six printings against two, November 1833 to July 1834 against February to April, and both trades. The brackets in the surviving name are the ink blot over the word after the ampersand in 1833-11-26 c030 and are kept as printed rather than tidied away.

'Doty & Co.' is 'H. Doty & Co.' with the forename initial lost, and one advertisement carries both. Both records are copy-dated April 29 1834 and both take the same store: 'Doty & Co.' at 1834-05-28 c008 reads 'the east end of South Water-s[treet] occupied by Peter Cohen, which they', and 'H. Doty & Co.' at 1834-06-04 c021 reads 'the [store at the] east end of South Water-street lately occupied by Peter Cohen' — the same sentence, the same taking-over of Cohen's store, a week apart, and the same trade in dry goods, groceries, crockery, clothing, boots and shoes. Merged INTO 'H. Doty & Co.' because that record is the one that can be placed: it carries the street on the business as well as in the offset and it prints the Cohen anchor twice more (1834-07-02 c010 and c057).

'P. Pruyne' is 'P. Pruyne & Co.' with the '& Co.' not set, and ONE advertisement is printed under both signatures. The timber notice copy-dated Ap'l. 22 runs on the '& Co.' side at 1834-04-23 c005 and 1834-04-30 c012 — 'THE subscribers having this day made an arrangement with Mr. A. McGregor … Pine Timber from 12 to 60 feet in length', signed '[P.] PRUYNE & CO.' — and on the other side at 1834-05-07 c012 as '[The] subscribers having this da[y] … from 12 to 60 f[eet] in [length,] from 6 to 14 in square. Thills supplied on short notice. Ap'l. 22. P PRUYNE'. Same opening words, same length range, same copy date, and a PLURAL subscriber over a singular signature. The house-for-sale notice at 1834-05-21 c001 carries the same copy date and the same plural — 'WE offer for sale the House on the corner of Lasalle and Lake streets' over 'Ap'l. 22. P. PRUYNE'. The surviving record already carries 'pine timber dealing' among its trades from the (timber) merge, so this is the third printing of a house the register had split three ways. Merged INTO 'P. Pruyne & Co.' because that is the record that can be placed: its store stands between Clark and Dearborn streets across four printings, while the other's live placement is `none`. ONE CAUTION THE MERGE CANNOT FIX HERE: the Lasalle-and-Lake corner it brings across is a house Pruyne OFFERS FOR SALE, not his own stand — 1834-05-21 c001 is a `building` claim and he signs it as vendor — so that reading must not be read as a second frontage for this firm. It does not become the live placement (its class outranks nothing, the source record's live placement being `none`), but it does stand in `placement_readings`, and T-0412 carries the machinery question.

firm_merges.from: Chicago Wholesale and Retail Book & Stationary Store
firm_merges.merge_rule: 'Chicago Wholesale and Retail Book & Stationary Store' is the first printing of the advertisement 'Russell & Clift' sign a week later, and the two are joined on the type rather than on the name. Chicago Democrat 1834-08-27 c002 and 1834-09-03 c012 carry the SAME copy date, “Chicago, Aug. 26, 1834”, the same heading, and the same body down to the stock “received from Philadelphia, and others from New York”; the later printing keeps the signature the earlier one lost with the woven half of its column, and signs it RUSSELL & CLIFT four times over the following months. The August printing therefore names no partner at all — it is declared a sign-name in `firm_sign_names` above and no claim signs it with a proprietor — which is the case T-0340 ruled on: an empty partner set does not contradict {Russell, Clift}. Merged INTO 'Russell & Clift' because that record carries the partners, the copartnership terms and the only placement either printing gives, adjoining Mr. P. Carpenter's drug establishment in Water-street; the direction is which record can be put on the ground.

firm_merges.from: Russell & Clift, Chicago Book and Stationary Store
firm_merges.merge_rule: 'Russell & Clift, Chicago Book and Stationary Store' is 'Russell & Clift' with the shop's sign run on after the partners, and the American prints the house that way through 1835: 1835-06-08 c015, 1835-06-13 c019, 1835-07-04 c006 and 1835-08-29 c005. Same two partners, same trade — books, stationery and the patent medicine agency the Democrat's own 1835-08-19 notice puts in the same hands — and no street on either side to contradict. The American gives no address in any of the four, so the merge takes Water-street from the record that has one and invents nothing. This is the same house continuing, not a second bookseller: the corpus names no other in Chicago in these years.

firm_merges.from: Russell & Clift, the Chicago Book Store
firm_merges.merge_rule: 'Russell & Clift, the Chicago Book Store' is 'Russell & Clift' under the premises the Democrat names for them on 1835-08-19 (c012): Morison's Hygeian medicine “for sale only by Russell & Cl[if]t (Agents for the State of I[ll]inois) at the Chicago Book Store”, signed RUSSELL & CLIFT and copy-dated Chicago, August 12, 1835 — the same agency the American's 1835-08-29 notice defends for the same firm ten days later. The partners agree without any declaration needed, because 'the Chicago Book Store' follows a comma in lower case and `firm_style` cuts it as a trade. NOTE what this merge carries across: that claim reads “Russell & Chin,” as a PROPRIETOR, so the firm's own name stands in the merged record's proprietor list beside Aaron Russell and Benj. H. Clift (T-0337 having joined the two readings of him). That is the gazetteer reading a partnership STYLE where a person was wanted — the case T-0359's `places` does not cover, filed as T-0398; nothing here edits a claim to hide it.

'P. F. W. Peck' is 'P. F. Peck' signed with the third initial of a fuller signature, and the two styles stand on ONE CORNER in windows that abut. The shorter style takes the corner of La Salle and South Water streets from 1833-12-03 c010 and keeps it through 1834-02-18 c008, 1834-03-04 c012 and 1834-06-18 c007; the longer style is copy-dated “1834-06-18” — the very issue in which the shorter one last appears — and runs from 1834-07-02 c023 through 1834-09-10 c005 to 1834-12-10 c011, reading “CORNER OF LASALLE AND F9UTH-WATER STB.” for the same corner. One general store either side of one week: dry goods, hardware, groceries and crockery on one side, dry goods, hardware, hollow ware, groceries, boots and shoes, saddlery, drugs, hats and ready made clothing on the other, and the second list is the first restocked. Merged INTO 'P. F. Peck' because that record carries the longer run, the copy date that dates the standing card, and the corner with both street names set out in full rather than abbreviated; the direction is which record can be placed, not which spelling is truer, and the fuller signature is kept verbatim in `merged`.

'F. G. Blanshard' is 'G. Blanshard' with the first initial printed, and the two styles are one standing advertisement read twice five weeks apart in one paper. The anchor is the same sentence both times: 'G. Blanshard' stands “opposite Dr. Temple's, Lake-st.” at 1834-10-08 c004, and 'F. G. Blanshard' stands “_eppasite Dr, Temple's, Hake,” at 1834-11-12 c012 — the same words through a damaged column. One trade, and it is not a trade two men would be printed in five weeks apart on one street: houses and lots for sale or to let. Merged INTO 'G. Blanshard' because that impression gives the anchor whole, with the street on it, while the November setting has to be read through the damage; the direction is which record can be placed, not which spelling is truer.

'G. W. Keeney' is 'W. Keeney' with the first initial printed, and the two styles are one standing advertisement read twice four weeks apart in the Democrat. The anchor is the same sentence both times: 'G. W. Keeney' reads “A fe[w] doors bel[ow] Messrs. N[ew]berry & Dole's” at 1834-05-07 c003, and 'W. Keeney' reads “A few doors below Messrs. Newberry & Dole's” at 1834-06-04 c022. One trade, word for word the same shop: tin, sheet iron and copper ware, cooking stoves, ploughs and mill castings. Merged INTO 'W. Keeney' because that impression carries the anchor with no bracketed supply in it, names the proprietor, and lists the whole stock — bells, cooking stoves, copper ware, hollow ware, mill castings, ploughs, sheet iron ware, tin ware — while the May setting names nobody; the direction is which record can be placed, not which spelling is truer, and the May trade string is kept in `trade_variants`.

'Dr. J. B. Barnard' is 'Dr. J. H. Barnard' with the second initial read out of a different setting, and the B and the H are the same letter of one physician's name. One lodging, printed twice nine days apart in two papers: the Democrat of 1835-06-04 c006 sets “AT THE MKW-YORK HOUSE, LaKE-sTRRET,” — read as “AT THE NEW-YORK HOUSE, LAKE-STREET” — over a copy date of 1835-06-03, and the American of 1835-06-13 c009 sets the same direction as “ar tie New Yous Horse, Lane atneet,”. One trade, and it is the same word: physician. Two physicians of one surname taking rooms in one hotel on one street inside nine days is not what the corpus shows; it shows one card carried by both papers. Merged INTO 'Dr. J. H. Barnard' because that record reads the address line whole and carries the copy date that dates the card, while the American's setting has to be read letter by letter; the direction is which record can be placed, not which spelling is truer.

'M. H. Kennicott' is 'Wm. H. Kennicott, Surgeon Dentist' with the Wm run together into an M, and the proof is not the name at all — it is that the two records are ONE STANDING ADVERTISEMENT and the later printing is copy-dated to the earlier one. The Democrat of 1835-08-05 c021 sets “DENTISTRY. OFFICE OPPOSITE THE EXCH[A]NGE, LAK[E]-STR[EET]. Doct. WM. H. [K]ENNICOTT, [S]URGEON DENTIST, who has practic[ed] in the above profession in this town for the past year, tenders his thanks to the citizen[s of] Chi[c]ago and vicinity for their liberal [p]a[tron]a[ge]” and copy-dates it “Jone 24.” — 1835-06-24. The Democrat of 1835-06-24 c007 is that issue, and it carries “[D]ENTISTRY. [AT] THE [ ], LAKE-STREET. M. H. KENNICOTT, [a] DENTIST, who has practiced [his] profession in this town for the [past …, returns] his thanks to the citizens of [Chicago and vici]nity, for their liberal patronage” — the same sentences in the same order, down to the free repairs for a year and the ladies attended at the office or at their residences, and the same street. The merge also repairs what the interleave ate: the June setting's address line lost the building's name between “AT THE” and “LAKE-STREET”, and the standing copy names it — the Exchange. Merged INTO 'Wm. H. Kennicott, Surgeon Dentist' because that record places the office against a landmark while 'M. H. Kennicott' can only be put in the street, and because the forename is printed there rather than run together; the direction is which record can be placed, not which spelling is truer. 'Surgeon Dentist' is declared a sign-name in `firm_sign_names` below, without which the capitalised designation reads as a second partner named Dentist.

firm_merges.from: L. Curtiss, attorney and counsellor at law
firm_merges.merge_rule: 'L. Curtiss, attorney and counsellor at law' is 'J. Curtiss' with the forename initial read as an L, and the two are one attorney's standing advertisement read twice — which the corpus settles on the copy date and the door rather than on the letter. Both are copy-dated 1835-05-18, and both stand first door west of Messrs. Jones, King & Co. in South Water street: the Democrat of 1835-05-20 c009 reads “O[FFICE] in South Water-street, first [door] west of Messrs. Jones, King & Co.”, and 1835-07-01 c013 reads “[first door] west of Messrs. Jones, [King & Co, (up] stairs.)”. One trade, to the word: attorney and counsellor at law, solicitor in chancery. One copy date, one door, one trade, six weeks apart — that is one card set twice, and no printing in this corpus puts two lawyers of this surname in that doorway. Merged INTO 'J. Curtiss' because that impression reads the whole direction, street and ordinal together, while the July setting survives only in supplies; the direction is which record can be placed, not which spelling is truer. THE REFUSAL AGAINST THE SURVEYOR IS RETARGETED IN THE SAME COMMIT (T-0413): 'L. Curtiss, attorney and counsellor at law' was the `into` side of a refusal against 'L. G. Curtiss', the deputy surveyor of Cook County, and that refusal is folded into the surviving one below rather than left to outlive its pair — the attorney is held apart from the surveyor exactly as before, on one record instead of two.

'Wm. G. Blanchard' is 'W. G. Blanchard' with the forename supplied whole out of a column that could not carry it, and the two are ONE standing advertisement read twice. The card is the same word for word in both impressions — “House and Land [Agent.] Lots purchased and Sold, or [by commission.] [1]2 Building Lots for sale, in th[e town and] School section. […] Houses to Let. Enquire at [the] Office on Lake st. opposite Dr. Temple's” at 1834-06-11 c008, and the same sentences with the same anchor at 1834-07-09 c025 — one trade, house and land agent, one street, one door. The surname was the thing that kept them apart and the corpus has now settled it against the reading: 1834-06-11 stood as 'Wm. G. Branchaud' on a supply made from two Tesseract-fallback columns, and T-0408 repaired that reading on the two impressions of this card whose columns are NOT fallbacks — 1834-07-16 line 5527 '1* G. BLANCHARD,' and 1834-09-17 line 3292 '[uncertain: BLALYCHARD,]'. What is LEFT is the forename form, 'Wm. G.' against 'W. G.', and that is the class this policy has always joined by declaration rather than by string: the firm rule holds a house to its PARTNER SURNAMES, which are the same one here, and T-0400 merged eight groups of exactly this shape. Merged INTO 'W. G. Blanchard' because that impression reads the anchor with its entity — Dr. Temple named and normalized — while the June setting survives through a fallback column that lost the proprietor line altogether; the direction is which record can be placed, not which spelling is truer.

firm_sign_names.style: Chicago Wholesale and Retail Book & Stationary Store
firm_sign_names.sign: Chicago Wholesale and Retail Book & Stationary Store
firm_sign_names.note: The whole style is the shop's sign and it names nobody. The 1834-08-27 Democrat printing of the copartnership notice kept the heading and lost the signature with the woven half of the column — the claim's own note records the address line reading “lue store is in brontese and homeo havel”, two columns of type on one row — so no proprietor is attributed to it by any claim, which is what the compiler checks before it will accept this. Left undeclared, `firm_surnames` reads 'Book', 'Store' and 'Wholesale' as three partner surnames that no printing ever carried.

firm_sign_names.style: Russell & Clift, Chicago Book and Stationary Store
firm_sign_names.note: The firm's own 1835 card in the American sets the partners over the sign: “Chicago Book and Stationary STORE. [R]USSELL & CLIFT have just rec[e]i[ved an a]dditional supply of [B]ook[s], Stationary, &c.” (1835-06-08 c015). The partner half is 'Russell & Clift'; the rest is the sign over the door. Undeclared, the comma-then-capital rule in `firm_style` cannot see the tail as a trade and the guard reports four partners — Book, Clift, Russell, Store — for a house with two.

The tail is the dentist's designation set in capitals under his own name, which is the shape `firm_style`'s comma-then-lower-case rule cannot see: the Democrat of 1835-08-05 c021 sets “Doct. WM. H. [K]ENNICOTT, [S]URGEON DENTIST, who has practic[ed] in the above profession in this town for the past year”, so the capitalised words after the comma are the trade the notice advertises and not a second partner. The partner half is 'Wm. H. Kennicott' and the claims sign the house with him — 'Kennicott, Wm. H.' — so this declaration takes nothing off the record that the printings put on it. Undeclared, `firm_surnames` reads two partners, Dentist and Kennicott, and the partner guard then refuses T-0413's merge of 'M. H. Kennicott' for a partnership no printing ever carried.

refused_firm_note: The REFUSALS the firm policy had no place for (T-0399). `firm_surnames()` groups the register on the partner surname alone, so it puts together houses that are not one house — a namesake, a trade word mistaken for a partner, one man's two unconnected trades — and until this section existed the only record of having judged such a group was the ABSENCE of a merge rule, which reads exactly like a group nobody has looked at yet. The next sweep then finds the group again and does the work again. A refusal is therefore declared as explicitly as a merge and held to the same disciplines: it names both spellings verbatim, it names the printings it rests on, and it cannot outlive its pair — a refusal whose two styles a later merge has collapsed is a judgement nobody can check and is a compile error. `kind` is one of three and the distinction is the point: `two_houses` (the papers show two), `not_joined` (one name, and no printing puts the two styles under one roof — which is not the same finding as two), `different_ground` (one house, and the papers put the styles in different streets, which is a removal and a removal is a claim). ONE REFUSAL RESTATED RATHER THAN RETIRED (T-1046). 'W. Montgomery' <- 'W. Montgomery, boot and shoe maker' held the auctioneer's house apart from the bootmaker's, and its stated ground was 'the bootmaker is L. W. Montgomery with the L lost in the setting'. That ground was true and this file was the only place the corpus said it: the READINGS still normalized the signature to 'W. Montgomery', so the gazetteer PERSON `person_w_montgomery` went on carrying 'boot and shoe maker' beside 'auctioneer', which no firm-level refusal can reach. T-1046 moved the judgement to where it belongs — the four impressions of the shoemaking notice now read L. W. Montgomery, on the L the 1834-03-04 c028 column preserves and the two whole signatures either side of it — and the refusal's `from` heading moved with them. IT WAS NOT DROPPED, and the reason is worth stating: `tools/adopt_street_faces.py` READS this section (T-0414). Its refusal 3 collapses one proprietor to one roof per face on the surname set alone, and a `two_houses` ruling is what makes it key on the TRADE instead — so without this row the auctioneer's own auction room is refused a street face because a Montgomery already stands on it. Repairing a conflation at the reading layer must not re-create it at the roof layer.

refused_firm_merges.refused_because: 'A. Garrett' and 'A. Garrett, auctioneer' are almost certainly one auctioneer and they are NOT one standing house, because the papers put the two styles on different ground and the move between them is a claim rather than a spelling. 'A. Garrett' takes a store in South-Water street near the bridge in December 1834 (1834-12-17 c001, 1834-12-24 c001); that stand is David Carver's old stand and W. Montgomery announces he has taken it in July 1835 (1835-07-08 c001); 'A. Garrett, auctioneer' is then selling Kankakee lots from Dearborn street in August 1835 (1835-08-22 c004). A firm that moved is documented by a removal notice, and this corpus does not yet hold one for Garrett — so the two frontages stay two records and the succession is read off the claims, not asserted by a merge.

refused_firm_merges.into: B. Jones, grocery and provision store
refused_firm_merges.refused_because: 'B. Jones, grocery and provision store' and 'B. Jones, storage and forwarding' are one man's two trades and no printing puts them under one roof — which is not the same finding as two men. The Democrat of 1833-11-26 sets them as two advertisements in two columns (c018 the grocery, c014 the forwarding notice soliciting for the opening of navigation in the spring), and neither gives an address; the grocery runs again at 1834-03-04 c022 with 'CHICAGO—ILLINOIS' for its whole direction. A merge here would assert a shared door the papers never state. Refused until a printing joins them.

'Jones & King' and 'Jones, King & Co.' are two firms, and the '& Co.' is the whole difference: it is a THIRD PARTNER, and the partner-surname guard cannot see him because it strips 'Co.' as a style suffix before it compares. Jones & King is Wm. Jones and Byram King, two partners, selling stoves and hollow ware from their store in Water-street near the bridge (1834-09-10 c008) and glass, sash and blinds priced at four cents (1834-12-03 c007, copy-dated Oct. 2, 1834). Jones, King & Co. is a firm announcing its own formation — 'The undersigned have formed a connection in the mercantile business, under the firm of Jones, King & Co.' — over THREE names, WILLIAM JONES, BYRAM KING and H. B. CLARKE, copy-dated May 26, 1835 (1835-05-27 c005) and standing again at 1835-07-08 c009 and 1835-07-29 c012. This project's own rule for firms is that a partnership IS its partners and a changed one is a different house; a copartnership notice is the strongest possible statement that they changed, and it is a claim about a new firm rather than a spelling of the old one. The succession from the one to the other is real — same two men, same hardware and stove trade, eighteen months apart — and it is read off the two notices, not asserted by a merge.

refused_firm_merges.into: J. D. Caton, attorney and counsellor at law
refused_firm_merges.refused_because: 'J. D. Caton, attorney and counsellor at law' and 'John Dean Caton' are one man read twice and they are NOT one standing office, because the papers put the two styles in different streets and nineteen months apart. The initialled style is the solo practice of December 1833, one door east of Brewster, Hogan & Co. in South Water Street (1833-12-17 c006) — the only printing in this corpus that puts Brewster, Hogan & Co. on a street at all. Between the two stands the partnership: Collins & Caton takes that same South Water frontage from January 1834 (1834-01-28 c007) and is still advertising in May 1835 (1835-05-20 c014). Only then does 'John Dean Caton' appear, in Dearborn Street, in July 1835 (1835-07-22 c003, 1835-07-29 c006). A practice that moved is documented by a removal notice and this corpus holds none for Caton, so the two frontages stay two records and the succession is read off the claims rather than asserted by a merge. The forename form is not what refuses this one — the ground is.

'John Wright' and 'J. Wright, merchant' are one surname with the forename whole against the forename initialled, and no printing puts them under one roof — which is not the same finding as two men. 'John Wright' is a Democrat advertiser from November 1833 to July 1834, cut nails from 3d to 20d (1833-11-26 c009) and then a New-York invoice of broadcloths, calicoes, crockery and groceries offered wholesale and retail (1834-07-02 c020, copy-dated May 28, 1834); his claims record the absence of an address as a fact — four advertisements in one issue and not one street. 'J. Wright, merchant' is an American advertiser twelve months later, in July 1835, selling sole and upper leather, salt and oak scantling (1835-07-11 c004), and he is on South Water Street because the auction room places itself east of him. Same town, same surname, different paper, a year's gap, and a different line of goods; nothing printed joins the two forms. Refused until a printing does.

'John H. Kinzie' and 'R. A. Kinzie' are two men of one family and the surname is the whole of what they share. The Kinzies are the largest family in the corpus and the Democrat of 1833-12-10 prints two of them on one page: 'Mr. R. A. Kinzie' stands in John Wellmaker's Man Trap notice (c008) and 'JAS. KINZIE' in a building notice beside it (c009). R. A. Kinzie's own card runs at 1834-02-18 c004 and 1834-03-18 c010, copy-dated 1834-02-17, and gives no trade beyond 'merchant'. John H. Kinzie is the forwarding and commission merchant of the ware house opposite Fort Dearborn, nine printings from 1834-04-16 c003 to 1835-07-29 c007, signing 'JOHN H. KINZIE' whole at 1834-05-07 c008. Two cards, two trades, two standing notices, and no printing joins them. One paper naming two men of a surname on one day is the plainest thing a surname group can be shown, and it is why nothing in this family merges on the name.

refused_firm_merges.from: John S. Kinzie, forwarding and commission merchant

To merge here is to assert that the '8' is an H, which is a repair to the page and not a reading of it; and the trade cannot do the joining either, because the note on the John S. card counts FOUR forwarding houses in the town that winter. The honest finding is that nothing joins them, and the page image is what would settle it.

'W. H. Brown' and 'Brown, painter' are two houses, and the painter's record carries no forename at all — which is exactly how a bare surname walks into a group it does not belong in. W. H. 'Wm. H. Taylor' and 'Charles Taylor' are two men, and both forenames are set on the page, so nothing here rests on a reading. Charles Taylor keeps a clothing and tailoring business in South Water street, Democrat 1834-06-04 c008. Wm. H. Taylor keeps a boot, shoe and leather store, wholesale and retail, in Dearborn street a few rods north of Messrs. Newberry & Dole's store, Democrat 1835-05-20 c020, copy-dated 1834-07-08. Two trades, two streets, and two forenames no compositor turns into one another.

'New York Clothing Store' and "Peter Cohen's store" share no partner at all. Both styles END in the word 'store', and `firm_surnames()` takes the last word of a partnership segment as the surname — so the group is made by a trade word and not by a partner. That is the failure being recorded, and it is not a near miss: the 'store' group holds thirteen of the register's businesses, everything whose style happens to end in the word, and it will re-form on the next sweep unless the function changes. On the printings the two are plainly separate. The New York Clothing Store is Tuthill King's clothing house, wholesale and retail, three doors north of an unread anchor in Dearborn Street, American 1835-06-08 c014 through 1835-07-04 c003. Peter Cohen's store is a South Water Street merchant's, Democrat 1834-01-07 c009, and it is the anchor L. W. Montgomery's bootmaking notice stands next door to. Eighteen months, two streets, two proprietors.

That is the failure being recorded, and it is not a near miss: the 'store' group holds thirteen of the register's businesses, everything whose style happens to end in the word, and it will re-form on the next sweep unless the function changes. Both styles END in the word 'store', and `firm_surnames()` takes the last word of a partnership segment as the surname — so the group is made by a trade word and not by a partner. Both stand in South Water Street and that is the one thing that makes this pair worth writing down rather than dismissing: the street cannot separate them, so the printings have to. refused_firm_merges.from: the new blacksmith shop opposite the Chicago Hotel
refused_firm_merges.refused_because: 'Eagle Hotel' and 'the new blacksmith shop opposite the Chicago Hotel' are not one house and they are not the same kind of thing. `firm_surnames()` grouped them on the word 'Hotel' — the last word of the first style, and the last word of the ANCHOR carried inside the second. An anchor mistaken for a partner is worth recording apart from the trade-word groups, because a style that names the building it stands opposite will always look like a partnership to a function that reads the last word, and the register holds more such styles than this one. The Eagle Hotel is P. B. F. Cable's and J. Shrigley's, four printings from 1834-04-16 c002 to 1834-10-08 c006. The blacksmith shop is Pierce and Abbott's, nearly opposite the Chicago Hotel, Democrat 1833-12-10 c011 and 1834-01-07 c007 — and the Chicago Hotel it names is a third house again, which is the point: the word in that style belongs to somebody else's signboard.

refused_firm_merges.from: The Chicago and St. Joseph packet, schooner Phillips
refused_firm_merges.refused_because: 'Chicago & St. Joseph Packet (schooner Llewellyn)' and 'The Chicago and St. Joseph packet, schooner Phillips' are two vessels on one route, not one house under two styles — and they are the clearest case in this file of a group made entirely of words. `firm_surnames()` splits on '&' and on 'and', so the route's own name yields 'Chicago' and 'packet' as its partners and every style naming the route joins the group. The Llewellyn is Clark's, master, advertised in the Democrat of 1835-05-27 c013 and copy-dated 1835-05-25, carrying freight and passengers between Chicago and the mouth of the St. Joseph. The Phillips is advertised nine months earlier, Democrat 1834-08-06 c007, with application on board or at the store of Messrs Newberry & Dole. A packet line names its schooner because the schooner is the thing that sails, and two names are two hulls.

'J. Curtiss' and 'L. G. Curtiss' are two men, and this one refusal now carries BOTH of the attorney's readings against the surveyor. 'J. Curtiss' is an attorney and counsellor at law and solicitor in chancery whose office is in South Water street, first door west of Messrs. Jones, King & Co.: the Democrat of 1835-05-20 c009, copy-dated 1835-05-18, and again at 1835-07-01 c013 over the same copy date and the same door, that second impression printing the forename initial as an L. 'L. G. Curtiss' is deputy surveyor of Cook County and takes his orders at the Mansion House, Democrat 1835-07-22 c012 and 1835-07-29 c015. A law office and a county surveyor's practice are two houses and no printing joins them; the G is printed, and the surname is dangerous here only because the attorney's own two settings disagree about his initial. WHY THIS REFUSAL IS ONE AND NOT TWO (T-0413): until this commit the July setting stood as its own style, 'L. Curtiss, attorney and counsellor at law', and was refused against the surveyor separately — the pair this group existed to trap, one initial apart and both read L. T-0413 merged that style into 'J. Curtiss' on the shared copy date and the shared doorway, so a refusal naming it would have outlived its pair, which this section calls a compile error. The judgement is unchanged and nothing is weakened: the attorney, under either initial, is still held apart from the surveyor, and the merge that joined his two readings did not touch the ground the surveyor stands on.
