refused_firm_merges.refused_because: 'J. Curtiss, Attorney and Counsellor at Law' and 'L. G. Curtiss, Deputy Surveyor of Cook County' are the signboard styles of the two houses held apart above, and the refusal is repeated on them because a refusal cannot reach a style it does not name. The Democrat of 1835-08-05 prints both in one issue: the attorney at c017, in South Water street at Jones, King & Co.'s store, and the surveyor at c011, with orders left at the Mansion House. One issue, one surname, two trades, two places.

refused_firm_merges.from: L. W. Montgomery, boot and shoe maker
refused_firm_merges.refused_because: 'W. Montgomery' and 'L. W. Montgomery, boot and shoe maker' are two houses and two men, and this is the trap the surname grouping was always going to set. The bootmaker is Loton W. Montgomery. His advertisement is copy-dated Dec. 15/18/19, 1833, places him next door to P. Cohen's store, and runs from 1833-12-17 c003 to 1834-04-08 c007 and beyond; it signs 'L. W. MONTGOMERY' wherever the type survives whole, and the damaged 1834-03-04 c028 column preserves the initial itself. 'W. Montgomery' is the auctioneer who takes David Carver's old stand in South Water street in July 1835 (1835-07-08 c001) and signs 'W. MONTGOMERY, Auc'r' (1835-07-22 c011) — a different trade, a different stand and eighteen months later. UNTIL T-1046 this row read `from: 'W. Montgomery, boot and shoe maker'` and gave as its ground that the bootmaker's L was lost in the setting; that was right, and the readings have now been repaired to say so, so the heading this row refuses has moved with them. The refusal itself stands unchanged in substance and is load-bearing: tools/adopt_street_faces.py reads a `two_houses` ruling to key refusal 3 on the trade rather than the surname alone, which is what stops these two Montgomerys taking each other's street face.

'W. G. Blanchard' and 'G. Blanshard' are one trade at one door and NO PRINTING IN THIS CORPUS SETS BOTH SPELLINGS, so the corpus cannot join them and this file will not join them on a resemblance. WHAT THE PAPER ACTUALLY SHOWS, and it is a great deal. Two land-agency cards run in the Chicago Democrat in 1834, one after the other and never in the same weeks: 'W. G. Blanchard' advertises “House and Land [Agent.] Lots purchased and Sold, or [by commission.] [1]2 Building Lots for sale, in th[e town and] School section. […] Houses to Let. Enquire at [the] Office on Lake st. opposite Dr. Temple's” (1834-06-11 c008, 1834-07-09 c025), and 'G. Blanshard' advertises “[HO]USES for [s]ale or to let. Also, a lot on the [cor]ner of Randolph and Wells streets, and [lots on the school section, which] will be sold [for cash. For particulars en]quire of [G. BLANSHARD], opposite Dr. Temple's, Lake-st.” (1834-10-08 c004, 1834-11-12 c012). The same landmark, the same street, the same business of selling town and school-section lots, and a gap between the two runs rather than an overlap. On the face of it that is one agent who changed his copy in the autumn, and this refusal says so rather than pretending the question is open. WHY IT IS STILL A REFUSAL. Both spellings are READ off the type and neither is a supply: 'BLANCHARD' is set in two columns the transcription does NOT flag as Tesseract fallbacks (1834-07-16 line 5527, 1834-09-17 line 3292) and 'BLANSHARD' is set whole in four impressions of its own card and again in the stray-horse reward notice of 1 October 1834 that runs beside it. So there is no misreading to repair, the way T-0408 repaired 'Branchaud' out of two fallback columns; there are two spellings the paper holds to, five weeks apart, and a forename initial that reads W in one card and F in the other. A shared anchor is two printings agreeing about a door, not one printing joining two styles — the distinction this section's `not_joined` kind exists to record, and the one C11 states for the town cards when it says a trade two men can share and a street two men can live on cannot carry an identification. The residents layer has already ruled the same way on the same initial: T-0993 holds `blanchard_w_g` distinct from `blanchard_f_gantry` under D1, noting that the Illinois land tract register carries no W. G. Blanchard at all. AND THE MACHINERY COULD NOT CARRY THE MERGE IN ANY CASE: `firm_surnames()` reads {blanchard} against {blanshard} and the partner guard refuses that with or without a rule, which is T-0407's question and not this one's. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: one printing that sets both spellings — the Democrat is caught doing exactly that for Blanshard, setting 'G. BLANSHARD' on 1834-10-01 and 'F. G. BLANSHARD' on 1834-10-22 in one standing notice — or a directory, poll or land-register entry that puts a W. G. Blanchard at the Lake Street office opposite Dr. Temple's.

premises_note: The THIRD ANSWER, for the pairs that are neither one house nor two unrelated ones (T-0411). `firm_merges` says two styles are one house; `refused_firm_merges` says they are not. The corpus keeps producing pairs for which both sentences are false — a paper and the shop that prints it, an agency and the house that keeps it — and T-0402 found it could write down no true thing about the first of them: `firm_surnames()` compares {democrat} against {office} and the partner-surname guard has no escape by design, while all three refusal kinds are untrue (these are not two houses; a printing DOES join them, the colophon being the paper naming its own shop; and in 1834 they stand on the same corner). So a relation is declared here instead, and it is NOT a merge: both records stay whole, keep their own printings, their own placement readings and their own trade, and the partner guard is untouched. It states one thing only, in one direction — the `part` is the `whole`'s premises or department — and it is held to the merge's disciplines: it names both spellings verbatim, it names the printings it rests on, it cannot outlive either end, it may not be declared alongside a merge or a refusal of the same pair, it may not run both ways, and a business may stand on one ground only. `kind` is one of two: `premises` (the part is the ground the whole is carried on — ONE roof, and the model must not mint a second for the whole) and `department` (the part is a branch of the whole's own business under a style of its own).

premises_relations.relation_rule: 'Chicago Democrat printing office' is the premises 'The Chicago Democrat' is printed at, and the two records are neither one business nor two unconnected ones. THE PAPER is read off its own imprint over John Calhoun's name, four printings between 1833-11-26 and 1834-12-03 placing it 'in the building on the corner of South Water and Clark-streets' (1833-11-26 c033, 1834-08-27 c009, 1834-09-17 c010, 1834-12-03 c023). THE SHOP is read off the paper's own colophon: 1834-01-07 c006 sets it in that same building on the corner of South Water and Clark streets, and 1835-05-20 c007 reads the colophon of that issue over Messrs. Jones & King's hardware store in the same street. WHY THIS IS NOT A MERGE: `firm_surnames()` reads the last word of each style as the partner surname and so compares {democrat} against {office}, and the partner-surname guard is right to refuse that — but neither style names a partner at all, so there is nothing here for the guard to be about, and loosening it for this pair would loosen it for every pair. WHY IT IS NOT A REFUSAL: none of the three kinds is true of it. They are not `two_houses` — one man, John Calhoun, stands over both records, and the paper and the shop that prints it are not two businesses of the town in any sense a walker would recognise. They are not `not_joined` — a printing joins them explicitly, because the colophon IS the paper naming the office it is printed at. They are not on `different_ground` — in 1834 both stand on the corner of South Water and Clark. Writing any of the three down would be a false judgement filed to make a group look closed, which is why T-0402 declined to file one. WHAT THE TOWN SHOWS, AND IT IS DECIDED HERE RATHER THAN LEFT TO FALL OUT: ONE ROOF. The roof already stands — `chicago_democrat_office`, 'The Chicago Democrat Office', which carries "John Calhoun's printing office" among its aka and is placed at that corner — and the shop enriches it. The paper did NOT: compile_register took `new_building` at `clark+south_water` for it, a second roof at the same corner for a business that has no ground of its own, because `match_occupant` requires ALL the partners' surnames and the paper's proprietors read ['John Calhoun', 'Calhoun, J.'] — a required set of {calhoun, j} that no occupant line can carry. The relation settles it: the whole follows its premises, the paper takes `enrich_existing` on `chicago_democrat_office`, and the register's actions move from 30 enrich_existing / 29 new_building to 31 / 28. WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE: T-0403, which records that the office keeps its 1834 corner through T-0399's internal merge because `placement_rank` prefers a corner to a relative offset regardless of date — so on the scene date of 1835-07-01 the shop may stand at the wrong end of South Water Street, and the paper now stands with it. That is a question about placement RANKING, not about identity, and it is left open here on purpose: joining the pair moves neither reading, and answering it would mean changing how every house in the register chooses its live address. T-0403 stays open.

anchor_note: The DATED ANCHOR CHANGE (T-0345), and it is the third thing two printings of one advertisement can differ about. `firm_merges` above joins two STYLES of one house and `proprietor_merges` joins two readings of one partner's name; neither can say that a house's printed ANCHOR changed on a date. Matthias Mason & Co.'s blacksmithing notice runs under a single copy date of 26 November 1833: to 1834-06-11 it reads 'on Main-street, nearly opposite Graves' Tavern', and from 1834-09-10 the same copy, word for word otherwise, reads 'opposite the Tremont House'. Held as two standing placements — which is what the register did — a placement sweep finds one shop in two places at once. What a declaration here may state is ONLY that two of a house's readings name two different landmarks rather than two spellings of one, and it must account for every reading the house carries. Everything else the compiler computes from the claims: the weeks each anchor was printed between, the order, the gap the change is bracketed by, and which anchor is live at the scene date. `cannot_say` is required and is the point of the whole thing — a change of anchor is not evidence of which side of it moved. AND IT IS ALSO WHAT A FIRM MERGE DEFERS TO (T-0403). `firm_merges` above hands the surviving record the higher-RANKED of two placements — a corner over a relative offset — and `placement_rank` is blind to the date on purpose, so a merge can leave a house at an address it had already left. The Chicago Democrat's printing office is that case and the two declarations below are its answer: the office's own colophon moves it off the corner of South Water and Clark streets and over Messrs. Jones & King's hardware store between 1834-01-07 and 1835-05-20, which is inside the scene, and the paper's imprint prints the same move on 1835-08-05, which is five weeks outside it and is therefore stated and not acted on. What makes the deferral safe is that a merge NARROWS NOTHING: every reading of both sides survives on the record, which is the only reason a rule here can be written afterwards at all.

anchors.name: Graves' Tavern
anchors.why: Four readings of one landmark, 'Graves' Tavern', differing only in how much of the street clause the reading pass carried into the anchor field and, once, in a lost apostrophe: 1833-11-26 keeps 'on Main-street' inside it, 1834-02-25 keeps 'Main-street', 1833-12-24 / 1834-01-07 / 1834-02-18 / 1834-03-04 / 1834-04-01 keep neither, and 1834-06-11 sets 'Gra]ves Tavern' across an interleaved line and loses the apostrophe with the preceding column. Every one of the seven is the same sentence of the same advertisement and every one names the same tavern; the street they differ over is carried in `street` and in each reading's own offset text, so no word is lost by grouping them. 1834-02-18 JOINED THIS GROUP AT T-0407 AND DID NOT MOVE ITS BOUNDARY. That impression had stood outside this house altogether, as a separate business called 'Matthias Nason & Co.', on a bracketed '[N]' its own transcription does not support — line 2823 of the 18 February setting reads MATTHIAS MASON & CO. whole and unmarked, and no impression of this notice reads an N. The supply is withdrawn in the claim. Its anchor was already the bare "Graves' Tavern" this group is about, so the printing lands inside the EARLIER anchor and the window this rule brackets — the change from the tavern to the Tremont House, between 1834-06-11 and 1834-09-10 — is untouched: 18 February 1834 adds a printing to the old anchor, not a date to the boundary.

anchor_changes.rule: Between 1834-06-11 and 1834-09-10 the anchor of this standing advertisement changes from "Graves' Tavern" to "the Tremont House" and the rest of the copy does not change with it — same 26 November 1833 copy date, same 'in all its various branches', same shoes and chains, same 'Work done on the shortest notice'. Two different landmarks, and this project holds both: Graves' Tavern is the log tavern modelled as `mansion_house` on the north side of Lake Street just east of Dearborn, and the first Tremont House stands at the north-west corner of the same crossing, some 36 m west of it. They are not two spellings of one house and they are not the same corner. The corpus carries no printing of this advertisement between those two dates, so the change is bracketed by them and no closer.
anchor_changes.cannot_say: WHICH SIDE OF THE STREET MOVED. Nothing printed anywhere in this corpus says whether the shop moved along Lake Street, or the house across from it changed hands and name, or a compositor was handed fresh copy for a reason nobody printed. All three would read exactly like this. The scene date is 1835-07-01, ten months after the later reading first ran, so the anchor live at the scene date is the Tremont House — that is a statement about the ADVERTISEMENT and not about the building, and the earlier anchor is kept with its own dates so a later pass can still tell the two cases apart. The reconstruction's own placement of `mason_blacksmith_shop` was set opposite `mansion_house` on the strength of the 1833-11-26 printing alone, and it has not been moved here: moving it would decide the question this note exists to leave open.

anchors.name: the corner of Franklin and South Water streets
readings: the corner of Franklin and South Water streets
the corner of Franklin and South Water-streets
anchors.why: Four readings of one crossing, 'the corner of Franklin and South Water streets', differing only in how much of the sentence the reading pass carried into the anchor field and, once, in what the ink left legible. 1833-12-17 / 1834-01-28 / 1834-03-04 / 1834-06-11 / 1834-08-20 / 1834-11-12 / 1834-11-26 and 1834-09-03 carry the words whole; 1834-05-28 drops the leading 'the corner of' and is read as a corner; 1834-07-09 hyphenates 'South Water-streets'; and 1834-10-15 sets the line so badly ('PEHICE second door vcot from tho corner ee / of Frankli s') that the reading could only carry 'the corner of Franklin [street]' with the second street name lost to the type. Every one of them is the same card, copy-dated 17 December 1833, counting the same two doors west from the same crossing, and the street each names is kept in its own reading, so no word is lost by grouping them.

anchor_changes.rule: Giles Spring's office card is reset once. From 1833-12-17 to 1834-11-26 every printing sets the office 'second door west from the corner of Franklin and South Water streets', on the copy date 17 December 1833. From 1835-05-20 the card is a different one — copy-dated 3 December 1834, seven days after the last printing of the old address — and it reads 'OFFICE, first door north from the Tremont House, on Dearborn-street'. These are two crossings of this town and not two spellings of one: Franklin and South Water is on the river's south bank at the west end of the business row, and the first Tremont House stands at the north-west corner of Lake and Dearborn, some four blocks east of it. The identity merge of 'Giles Spring' into 'G. Spring' already reads both cards off the page and says the second one moves him; this rule is that reading applied to the placement, not a new judgement. The corpus carries no printing of either card between 1834-11-26 and 1835-05-20, so the change is bracketed by those two dates and no closer — with the copy date of 3 December 1834 saying only when the new card was WRITTEN, which is not the same as when the office moved.
anchor_changes.cannot_say: WHEN THE OFFICE ACTUALLY MOVED, AND WHETHER IT MOVED AT ALL. A card copy-dated 3 December 1834 that first appears in this deposit on 20 May 1835 leaves five and a half months in which nothing printed here says where Spring sat; the deposit is not the paper's whole run, so the new address may have been printed weeks or months before the issue that carries it, and the old one may have gone on running beside it in issues this project does not hold. Nor does anything printed say that ONE office moved rather than that a lawyer who had rooms on South Water Street took rooms on Dearborn Street: both would read exactly like this. What the rule decides is only which anchor the card is printed under at the scene date of 1835-07-01 — the Tremont House, first printed 20 May 1835 and printed again 5 August 1835 — and that is a statement about the ADVERTISEMENT. The earlier anchor is kept with its own dates and its own eleven printings so a later pass can still tell a removal from a second office. The Dearborn address is itself a count of doors, 'first door north from the Tremont House': it fixes a side of Dearborn Street and an order along it, not a lot width, and no lot is claimed for it here.

anchors.name: the corner of South Water and Clark streets
readings: the corner of South Water and Clark streets

anchor_changes.rule: THE PAPER'S OWN COLOPHON, TWICE, AND IT DOES NOT SAY THE SAME THING BOTH TIMES. 1834-01-07 c006 reads the Democrat's imprint 'in the building on the corner of South Water and Clark streets'; 1835-05-20 c007 reads the colophon of that issue 'over Messrs. Jones & King['s] Hard[ware store]', South Water street. Two different landmarks and not two spellings of one: 'the corner of South Water and Clark streets' is a platted crossing this project holds, and "Messrs. Jones & King's hardware store" is a house of business in the same street, carried in this corpus as business_jones_king_co. A printing office is not in a crossing and over a hardware store at the same time, so between 1834-01-07 and 1835-05-20 the office's printed address changed, and the corpus brackets the change by those two dates and no closer: no printing of this colophon between them has been read. THE CORPUS SAYS WHY, in the OTHER Democrat record rather than in this one — chicago_democrat_1834_10_08 c005 offers 'the store now occupied by W. Kimball, and as the office of the Democrat' for sale with possession in November 1834, which is a landlord's notice and not this shop's own reading, so it is cited here and claims no anchor here. The scene date is 1835-07-01, six weeks after the later colophon first ran, so the anchor live in the scene is the hardware store.
anchor_changes.cannot_say: WHICH HOUSE, AND WHERE IN THE STREET. "Messrs. Jones & King's hardware store" is an anchor this corpus cannot resolve to ground: business_jones_king_co prints South Water Street and nothing narrower, and business_jones_king prints 'their store in Water-street, near the bridge', an anchor the committed town does not hold. So this rule moves the office OFF the corner of South Water and Clark streets and does not put it anywhere in particular — South Water Street, over a store whose own address the papers never fix. That is a loss of precision and it is the honest reading: the narrower address was the older one. NOR DOES IT SAY WHAT BECAME OF THE BUILDING. data/structures/chicago_democrat_office.json stands at the corner on the 26 November 1833 imprint and on Andreas, and a building does not move when its tenant does; nothing here touches its coordinate. WHAT IT LEAVES OPEN is whether 'over Jones & King's' is a separate building at all or the same corner block under a new ground-floor tenancy — c007 says 'over', which is a floor, and no printing reached gives that store's corner. The paper itself, business_the_chicago_democrat, still stands at the crossing in this register because the only printing of the move IT carries is 1835-08-05, five weeks outside the scene; joining the two records is T-0411's and is deliberately not done here.

anchors.name: the corner of South Water and Clark streets
readings: the corner of South Water and Clark streets
corner of Clark and South Water streets
anchors.why: Two readings of one crossing, 'the corner of South Water and Clark streets', differing in the order the two street names were set and in the leading article. The imprint sets them in that order on 1833-11-26 c033, 1834-08-27 c009, 1834-09-17 c010 and 1834-12-03 c023; 1834-10-08 c005 is a for-sale notice about the same premises and sets 'on the [corner] of Clark an[d] South Water [s]tr[e]ets'. A crossing has no canonical order of its two streets and this project's own street key holds one crossing of clark and south_water, so calling these one landmark takes nothing away; each reading keeps its own words, dates and claims below.

anchor_changes.rule: THE SAME MOVE AS THE COLOPHON'S, WITNESSED FIVE WEEKS TOO LATE TO PLACE THIS RECORD. Every reading of the paper's own imprint through 1834-12-03 gives 'the corner of South Water and Clark streets'; 1835-08-05 c026 gives "Jones & King's hardware store". Two different landmarks, bracketed between 1834-12-03 and 1835-08-05 — a platted crossing and a house of business in South Water Street, and a paper is not printed at both. The change is real and this rule states it. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO IS PLACE THIS RECORD ON IT. The later anchor was first printed 1835-08-05, five weeks after the scene date 1835-07-01, and AGENTS.md rule 3 refuses an address to a town that had not read it yet; the compiler computes the live anchor from the windows and leaves this record at the crossing for that reason alone, which is what `live_reason` says. This declaration exists so that the reason is IN the record: before it, this house sat at the corner with nothing to say that its own paper had printed a different address, and a reader could only find that out by reading business_chicago_democrat_printing_office.
anchor_changes.cannot_say: WHETHER THE SCENE BOUND IS RIGHT ABOUT THIS HOUSE, and the corpus is in two minds because it keeps the Democrat as two records. The paper's own printing office carries the same move from 1835-05-20, six weeks INSIDE the scene, and is placed on it; this record's only printing of it is 1835-08-05 and is refused. So on 1835-07-01 the register stands the office over the hardware store and the paper at the crossing, which is not two premises but two extractions of one shop — the relation the gazetteer cannot express and T-0411 is open on. Nothing here forces them together: merging on the strength of this would decide T-0411 by side effect, and weakening the scene bound to let an August printing place a July town would decide it for every house in the corpus. NOR DOES IT SAY WHICH SIDE MOVED — 1835-08-05 is a fire-insurance card and the corner readings are a masthead, so the two are not even the same kind of statement about an address, and nothing printed says whether the press moved, the building changed hands, or a compositor was handed fresh copy.

refused_anchor_note: THE REFUSAL OF A DATED ANCHOR CHANGE (T-0773, landed by T-0949), and it is `anchor_changes`' own argument kept the other way up. `tools/measure_placement_silence.py` counts the houses whose live placement one of their own later printings OUTRANKS, and reordering two printed addresses is a judgement only a rule above may make. Some of that population must never get one — and the only record of that was the ABSENCE of a rule, which reads exactly like a house nobody has looked at yet, so the next sweep finds the same houses and reads them again. A refusal is therefore declared as explicitly as a change, and the compiler checks its KIND against the readings rather than taking the author's word: `printed_in_the_same_weeks` has to overlap, `silence_is_not_an_anchor` has to have a live placement that names no anchor, and `after_the_scene_date` has to have every outranking printing first set after 1835-07-01. Each refusal names verbatim an anchor it refuses to be reordered by, and a refusal whose pair has gone — a house no printing outranks any more — is an error here rather than a line nobody notices has stopped being true. THAT LAST GUARD IS WHY THERE ARE TWO ENTRIES HERE AND NOT T-0773's FIVE. Between T-0773's reading and T-0949's landing, T-0440, T-0859 and T-0948 each repaired part of the population: `business_j_s_c_hogan` and `business_newberry_dole` were held by printings that named no ground at all and T-0440 now places both, and `business_rockwell_cabinet_furniture_warehouse` is narrowed by T-0948 on its own street under its own dateline. Nothing outranks any of the three any more, so a refusal for them would be a judgement about nothing and the compiler says so. The two below are the ones whose pair still stands. `silence_is_not_an_anchor` is therefore declared by no house today and is kept because it is the kind the next silent-then-anchored house will need; its guards are asserted in `compile_gazetteer.py`'s self-test.

refused_anchor_changes.refused_because: T-0324 read every printing of both of this house's addresses and settled them: "next door to Graves' Tavern" and "the corner of Dearborn and Lake streets" are ONE frontage — not two premises, and not a move. Both run in a single issue, 1834-04-01 c009 and c010, six weeks after the move a reordering would have to record; and through that whole stretch the corner card is being re-set with fresh date lines, Feb 4 then Feb 24 then Apr 22, while the tavern card keeps running, which is not what a man does with an advertisement he has forgotten to pull. Graves' Tavern is itself that corner: it is the Mansion House, held in this reconstruction since 2026-08-11 on the north side of Lake Street just east of Dearborn. So these anchors have no before and no after to be put in, and a rule may only be written where one anchor stops before the next starts — any dates such a rule stated here would be false whatever it said about the ground. docs/RESEARCH/botsford_graves_1834.md is the reading and its table is the evidence.

Every printing this house has runs after the scene date, the earliest on 1835-07-22, and the one that outranks the rest is the last of them: 1835-08-12 reads 'call at [h]i[s] room [in] South [Wa]ter street, (A. Garrett's Auction Room)'. So the narrower address is six weeks outside the scene, and AGENTS.md rule 3 refuses it there for the same reason it refuses the address that would have placed Jones, King & Co. The South Water Street of the 1835-07-22 card is what the house keeps. T-0948 reached this house and declined it too, on two grounds of its own — two datelines are two advertisements, and the 08-12 reading names no street to be narrowing one — so what is missing here is not a judgement between two printed addresses. It is a printing inside the scene.

proprietor_note: The PROPRIETORS' half of the same policy (T-0337), and the last of the three places a name lives here. `merges` governs gazetteer PERSONS and `firm_merges` governs business STYLES; a proprietor is neither — it is a string on a business record, put there by whichever claim read that printing, so one man read two ways became two proprietors of his own house and nothing in either policy could reach across to say so. `business_russell_clift` carried 'Benj. Clift' from the 1834-09-03 impression of the copartnership notice and '[H. H.] Clift' from the 1834-11-12 impression of the SAME notice. The rule is the firm-side sibling of the person one and it points the other way on purpose: for a person, same surname with different initials never merges, silently and by default, because the letter lists are full of families; for two proprietors of ONE house the default cannot be silence either way, because brothers really do trade together — William and Franklin Brewster sign one dissolution notice — and so does one man read twice. So the compiler REFUSES any pair of person-styled proprietors of one house that share a surname and carry different, read forename initials, until it is declared: `proprietor_merges` joins two readings of one name, `proprietor_distinctions` holds two men apart, and each carries its reasoning. A bare surname beside a full name is not a pair — that is the papers printing less, not a second man — and a declaration whose pair has gone is refused too, so these cannot rot.

proprietor_merges.merge_rule: '[K.] Botsford' is 'J. K. Botsford' with the first initial cut off the line. Both are readings of the one Chicago merchant this corpus carries under that surname: the house advertises in twenty claims across 1834 and every impression that sets the name whole sets 'J. K. Botsford'. Nothing in the corpus names a second Botsford, so there is no second man the shortened style could belong to.

'[J.] K. Botsford' is 'J. K. Botsford' with the first initial supplied by the transcriber rather than printed — a bracketed letter is a letter read through and restored, which is a correction and not a difference. Same house, same trade, same surname, and no second Botsford anywhere in this corpus.

'E. Wentworth' is 'H. E. Wentworth' with the first initial lost off the front of the line. It is one standing advertisement, not two: the tavern-keeper's notice of 1833-12-17 ('PUBLIC HOUSE, H. E. WENTWORTH, has opened a TAVERN on Flag Creek') runs again on 1834-01-07 word for word, down to the corn and oats kept on hand, and the second impression sets the name 'E. WENTWORTH'. One house on Flag Creek, one keeper, one insertion running about eight months.

'P. S. Carli' and 'P. J. Carli' are one man, and the middle letter is the only thing between them. It is one advertisement twice printed: 1834-06-18 sets 'A FEW setts of elegant fancy Chairs and Rocking Chairs. Also, some Harnesses and Saddles. Enquire of P. J. CARLI, Eagle Tavern' and 1834-09-10 sets the same chairs, rocking chairs, harnesses and saddles over 'P.5.CARLI, Eagle Tavern' — a printing whose own middle character reads as the DIGIT 5, so that letter is not legible in this advertisement. The Eagle is the same house in both and the corpus names no second Carli.

'M. Jones' is 'Wm. Jones' with the W and the m run together, which is what the 1834-07-09 impression prints: 'M, JONES,' — a comma where the abbreviation's stop belongs. The firm is the same in both readings and so is the other partner: the stove and hollow-ware house of Jones & King, signed 'M, JONES, BYRAM KING' on 1834-07-09 and carried as Wm. Jones and Byram King from 1834-09-10, and the successor firm's own card of 1835-05-27 signs 'WILLIAM JONES, BYRAM KING, H. B. CLARKE'. This corpus names no second Jones in the partnership.

'Clarke, W. B.' is 'H. B. Clarke' with the first initial misread. It is one advertisement three times printed: the Jones, King & Co. connection notice sets 'WILLIAM JONES, BYRAM KING, H, B, CLARKE' on 1835-05-27 and 'WILLIAM JONES, BYRAM KING, H. B. CLARKE' on 1835-07-08, and the 1835-08-05 impression of the same three signatures in the same order reads 'WB. CLARKE.' — a printing whose first signature it also mangles to 'WILLEAAL JONES,'. Same firm, same partners, same week's standing insertion; the second initial B is common to every reading.

'Mathias Mason & Co.' is 'Matthias Mason & Co.' with one T dropped, and the pair exists in this house's proprietors only because the firm merge above unioned the 1834-09-10 impression's list into it. Ten of the eleven printings of this advertisement set MATTHIAS; the eleventh brackets the letter it could not read.

'P. F. W. Peck' is 'P. F. Peck' with the third initial of the merchant's fuller signature printed, and the pair exists in this house's proprietors only because T-0413's firm merge unioned the two styles' lists into one. Both are the same signature on one general store at the corner of La Salle and South Water streets, in windows that abut on the issue of 1834-06-18 — the last the shorter style is printed in and the copy date the longer one carries. The corpus names no second Peck merchant on that corner, and no printing sets the two initials against each other as two men.

'F. G. Blanshard' is 'G. Blanshard' with the first initial printed, and the pair exists in this house's proprietors only because T-0413's firm merge joined the two styles. It is one advertisement set twice in one paper five weeks apart — “opposite Dr. Temple's, Lake-st.” at 1834-10-08 c004 and the same words damaged at 1834-11-12 c012 — offering houses and lots for sale or to let both times. One man read with and without his first initial, not two Blanshards on one Lake Street frontage.

'J. B. Barnard' is 'J. H. Barnard' with the second initial read out of a second setting, and the pair exists in this house's proprietors only because T-0413's firm merge joined the two styles. The Democrat of 1835-06-04 c006 and the American of 1835-06-13 c009 carry one physician's card nine days apart, both lodging him at the New-York House in Lake Street; the B and the H are one letter printed twice, and the register holds no other Barnard practising in the town.

'M. H. Kennicott' is 'Kennicott, Wm. H.' with the Wm of the printed forename run together into an M, and the pair exists in this house's proprietors only because T-0413's firm merge joined the two styles. The 1835-08-05 printing that signs itself “Doct. WM. H. [K]ENNICOTT, [S]URGEON DENTIST” is copy-dated “Jone 24.” — the Democrat of 1835-06-24, which is the issue that prints 'M. H. KENNICOTT'; one standing advertisement, sentence for sentence, and one dentist on Lake Street in it.

'L. Curtiss' is 'J. Curtiss' with the forename initial read as an L, and the pair exists in this house's proprietors only because T-0413's firm merge joined the attorney's two styles. Both printings are copy-dated 1835-05-18 and both put the office first door west of Messrs. Jones, King & Co. in South Water street (1835-05-20 c009, 1835-07-01 c013) in one trade, attorney and counsellor at law and solicitor in chancery. The third Curtiss the corpus carries, 'L. G. Curtiss' the deputy surveyor, is a different man and stays a different record: he is held apart in `refused_firm_merges`, his G is printed, and his orders are left at the Mansion House.

proprietor_distinctions.rule: Two men, and the paper says so in one sentence: the dissolution notice of Brewster, Hogan & Co. is signed 'WILL[IAM BREWSTER,] FRAN[KLIN BREWSTER,] JOHN [S. C. HOGAN.]' (1834-06-11 c001, the bracketed supplies read off the 1834-06-18 printing of the same notice). Two Brewsters sign as partners of one house, so William Brewster and Franklin Brewster are two partners and not two readings.

Two men, named as two in the firm's own style. The dissolution notice of 1834-07-02 reads 'The copartnership heretofore existing between G. W. & William Laird, under the firm of G. W. & W. Laird' and is signed 'G. W. LAIRD, WM. LAIRD' — the style itself carries both partners, and the books are left in the hands of G. W. Laird alone, which only means something if the other is somebody else.

Two men, printed one under the other over their own firm's card: 'HUBBARD & CO. Commission and Forwarding MERCHANTS, CHICAGO—ILLINOIS. GURDOs S. HUBBARD, HENRY G. HURBARD.' (1835-07-01 c016). Gurdon S. Hubbard and Henry G. Hubbard sign as two partners of one house, and the Newberry & Dole card of 1835-08-05 names them separately again.

Two men — and T-0396 SETTLES WHICH OF THEM STOOD IN THE FIRM (2026-09-12): not Oliver Newberry. 'Oliver Newberry' and 'Newberry, [Walter L.]' are held apart on the corpus's own evidence, and the evidence that holds them apart also decides the partner. THE FIRM'S OWN PAID CARD PRINTS OLIVER NEWBERRY IN ITS REFERENCE LIST, UNDER DETROIT, in every setting that names him: 'Oliver Newberry, [Det]roit' (1834-04-01 c013) and 'OLIVER NKWBERRY, Detroit.' (1835-07-01 c015), each standing in a list of one correspondent per port — Coenties Slip in New York, Barker & Holt of Buffalo, Calvin Britain at the mouth of the St Joseph, James B. Campbell at Ottawa. Both claims give his role as a reference named in the advertisement, and neither gives him a trade. A house does not print its own resident partner as the man to write to in another city. THE 1835-08-05 SETTING (c022) HOLDS BOTH AT ONCE, which is what makes this a decision rather than a preference: the partner entity reads 'NEWRERRY', normalized 'Newberry, [Walter L.]', role `partner`, occupation forwarding and commission merchant, while 'Oliver Newb[err]y, Detro[it]' still stands in the same card's reference list four names below it. One notice, two Newberrys, one of them the house and the other its correspondent. AGAINST THAT stands only the received identification on the 1834-03-04 reading (c021) — which prints NO FORENAMES at all, and whose own note says the identification is received rather than read — and Andreas's 'Oliver Newberry and George W. Dole' at scan p. 1151, set in 1884. A compiler writing half a century later, and a reading that says in terms it is not reading, do not outweigh the firm's own paid advertisement: the advertiser paid for it and his customers had to be able to find him. WHICH Newberry, then, is the weaker limb and is INFERRED, not documented: Walter L. Fergus 1839 prints 'Newberry, Walter L., att'y and real est., office Newberry & Dole' — the firm's office as his office; the American of 1835-06-08 (c004) prints 'W. L. NEWBERRY' over the great sale of town lots and sets 'NEWBERRY & bOUJ' — Newberry & Dole — over the same date in the adjacent column of the same issue, and that claim's note already reads the one off the other; and no other Newberry forename is printed for Chicago anywhere in this corpus. THE ONE RIVAL LEFT UNRESOLVED IS NOT A PRINTING: the land register's WALTER S / W S, which no volume of this corpus prints — data/research/land_sales/README.md § The two Newberrys the register writes. THE DECLARATION STAYS because both readings are still proprietors of this house on the record and the gate is right to ask; what has changed is that it now says which is which. Nothing here regrades hh_newberry_walter_loomis, mints a trade or places a premises: the two structure records newberry_dole_warehouse and newberry_dole_slaughterhouse_south_branch carry the ruling on their `occupants` at `inferred`, and grading against every source at once is T-0515's pass.

place_note: The third case, and it is not a third kind of merge (T-0359). A claim's entities are keyed on a name and carry no notion of WHAT a name is, so a building the papers name by its signboard — "Haddock's Tavern", "the Eagle Hotel", "the Baptist meeting house" — is minted into the persons table and then held to a policy written for people. The compiler reads "Tavern" as the surname and "Haddock's" against "Maddock's" as forename initials, and the families rule refuses a reconciliation the evidence closes. The families rule is right; the subject is wrong. `places` is therefore where a name is declared NOT to be a person, one entry per name and each with the argument written out, and `place_merges` joins two spellings of one building afterwards. Nothing here loosens the families rule: a place merge may only join two names `places` has already argued are not people, and a name whose every mention is a post-office letter list may not be declared a place at all — a letter list is a list of people somebody wrote to, and "Chester House" and "Rodney House" in `refused_places` are exactly that shape. A name carrying an occupation is refused too, because a claim is reading it as a person. Both refusals are compile errors, not conventions.

places.name: Haddock's Tavern
places.why: "Haddock's Tavern" is a building, not a man. It is minted out of G. Spring's standing For-Sale notice, which sells a lot BY it — "Lot No. 7, in block No. 16, one lot east of Haddock's Tavern, on Lake street" (chicago_democrat_1834_11_19 c010, and the same copy at 1834-06-18, 1834-09-03 and 1834-10-15). The name is doing placement work: it is the landmark the lot is measured from. The man behind the signboard is in this corpus separately and under his own name — E. Haddock, at whose house the Board of Trustees met on 6 June 1834 (1834-06-18 c002), H. Haddock of the Fourth of July notice (1834-06-25 c002), E. H. Haddock of the election notice (1834-07-30 c003) — so declaring the signboard a place removes a duplicate of the building, not the person.

places.name: Maddock's Tavern
places.why: "Maddock's Tavern" is the same signboard as Haddock's Tavern, set once with an M, and it is a building either way. It is minted out of the 1834-07-09 setting of G. Spring's For-Sale notice (c024), which is the same advertisement, dated the same June 18, selling the same Lot No. 7 in block No. 16 one lot east of it on Lake street. It is declared a place for the reason its four sibling settings are: the name is the landmark the lot is measured from, not a person the paper is writing about. Which of the two spellings the printer set is settled in `place_merges`, and could not be while the compiler read the word Tavern as a surname.

places.name: Eagle Hotel
places.why: "Eagle Hotel" is a house of entertainment, and the claim that mints it (chicago_democrat_1834_05_14 c008) sets it as a display heading over its own advertisement — the building advertising itself. It is a sign and not a person: no forename or initial is ever printed as PART of it. A keeper's name is a different thing, and the house carries those — Steele's in February 1834, the taker of 15 April 1834, J. Shrigley from 1 September 1834 — which is why "the Eagle Hotel (Steele's)" merges into this record under T-0391 rather than standing beside it.

places.name: the Eagle Hotel (Steele's)
places.why: "the Eagle Hotel (Steele's)" is a building named with its keeper in a parenthesis — the 1834-02-04 notice (c003) locates something at "the Eagle Hotel, (Steele's)", which is an address and not a person's name. It is declared a place on that reading alone, and THAT DECLARATION IS WHAT MAKES THE MERGE POSSIBLE: `place_merges` may only join two names this table has already argued are not people. Whether it and "Eagle Hotel" are one house was left open here until T-0391, and it is now answered in `place_merges` and not here — on the 1834-02-04 issue setting the name three times in one column, twice without a keeper, and on the succession of keepers the corpus follows through that one house. It was not answered on the shared word Eagle, which this file exists to refuse.

places.name: the Baptist meeting house
places.why: "the Baptist meeting house" is a building and reads as one in plain words — the 1834-05-21 claim (c003) puts it in South Water Street, which is already recorded on the entry as an associated place. It is a congregation's house, not a person, and no printing gives it a forename because none exists.

place_merges.merge_rule: "Haddock's Tavern" and "Maddock's Tavern" are one building, and G. Spring's own advertisement is the witness that says so. One notice, dated June 18 1834 and standing over five settings, sells Lot No. 7 in block No. 16, one lot east of the tavern, on Lake street, with a large dwelling-house and fine well on it. Four of the five settings read Haddock's (1834-06-18 c006, 1834-09-03 c005, 1834-10-15 c006, 1834-11-19 c010) and exactly one reads Maddock's (1834-07-09 c024). That is the condition the 1834-07-30 reading pass set for closing this: an issue printing both spellings in a way that decides it. Four settings of one advertisement against one is that. The direction is into the reading four settings carry, and the corpus corroborates it outside the notice — E. Haddock kept the Mansion House and the Board of Trustees met there (1834-06-18 c002), while no Maddock appears anywhere in these papers. This merge is possible only because both names are declared places: as persons the families rule refused it, reading Tavern as a surname and H against M as forename initials, which is a rule for a family of people applied to a signboard. T-0324 found it, T-0359 could record it.

"Eagle Hotel" and "the Eagle Hotel (Steele's)" are one house, and the issue of 1834-02-04 is the witness that decides it — the condition this pair was held open for. Page 3, column 3 of that issue sets the name THREE TIMES in one compositor's column, twice without a keeper: at lines 2251-2260 the citizens of Chicago are called to meet "at the Ea[g]le Hotel, (Steele's)" (claim c003); ten lines below, at 2270-2281, the citizens of Cook county are called "to m[e]et [a]t the Eagle Hotel in Chicago" (c004); and at 2310-2320 an auction is cried "at the [Eag]le Hotel in this town" (c006). The setting WITH the parenthesis and the setting WITHOUT it stand ten lines apart in one column, and the two bare ones are qualified by the TOWN — "in Chicago", "in this town" — which is a paper distinguishing its Eagle from Eagles elsewhere and not from a second Eagle at home. A compositor holding two houses of one name apart for his own readers does not set the second and third without a word to tell them from the first.

AND THE SUCCESSION SAYS IT INDEPENDENTLY. The corpus follows one house it calls "the Eagle Hotel", with the definite article, through named keepers and no break: Steele's in February 1834; "he has taken the EAGLE HOTEL" over a copy date of 15 April 1834 (1834-04-16 c002, reprinted 1834-05-14 c008, 1834-06-18 c014, 1834-07-02 c004), which is a succession notice and not a building notice — the taker is a new keeper of a house that already stood; and "P. J. CARL[I], having relinquished the tav[e]rn known as the Ea[g]l[e] Hotel, on the [first of] [S]eptember last, to J. Shrigley" (1834-10-08 c006). "Known as" is the paper's own statement that the house is a single known one. The keeper who took it in April is read "P. B. F. CABLE" in some impressions and "P. J. [CARLI]" in others; WHICH the type carries is a separate question and this merge neither touches nor needs it.

SO THE PARENTHESIS IS A KEEPER, NOT A SIGN, and it is an idiom this paper uses: it writes "the Eagle Coffee House, Trowbridge's" (1835-06-24 c001) and the town carries "Graves' Tavern" the same way. The direction is into the sign, because "Eagle Hotel" is what the house sets over its own advertisement (1834-05-14 c008) while a keeper's name lasted seven months.

WHAT THIS MERGE DOES NOT REACH, stated so the next reader does not extend it. The EAGLE COFFEE HOUSE — "Trowbridge's", also "the Eagle House" — is a DIFFERENT house and is not joined here: it appears only from 1835-06-24, in or about Dearborn Street (1835-06-24 c006, 1835-08-05 c020), with its own keeper, while the Eagle Hotel is placed nowhere in the whole of 1834 and no notice gives it a street. Two houses of entertainment may share a bird. "Eagle Precinct, Lasalle county" (1834-07-30 c008) is not in Chicago at all. T-0391.

refused_places.name: Chester House
refused_places.refused_because: "Chester House" is a person, not a building, and the shape of the evidence says which. Both its mentions are post-office lists of letters remaining uncalled-for (1834-04-01 c001, 1835-05-20 c013) and one of them prints it inverted — "House, Chester" — which is the surname-first setting those columns use. The surname is House and the forename is Chester. He is one of the twelve names the letter lists put into the town's households on 2026-08-29, and declaring him a place would delete a resident. The compiler refuses it independently of this note: every mention is a letter list.

refused_places.name: Rodney House
refused_places.refused_because: "Rodney House" is a person for the same reason "Chester House" is. Its one mention is the 1834-04-01 letter list (c001), it stands in a column of people the post office was holding letters for, and House is the surname. No claim in this corpus puts a Rodney House on a street or over a door. The compiler refuses the declaration independently of this note.

agency_note: AN AGENCY IS A RELATION AND NOT A HOUSE (T-0410). A business record holds a trade, goods, proprietors, a street and placement readings; an agency is none of those. It is a relation between a principal that is not in this town at all and a local house or man who holds it for a season, and until this section existed the corpus could express it only by minting the agency as its own business — which then collided with the house holding it under `firm_surnames()` and had to be refused by hand. A declaration here names the principal, records who held the agency over what window, and may RETIRE the business record the corpus minted for the agency itself. The window is COMPUTED from the witnesses' own issue dates and may not be asserted. What a holding may never do is the reason this section exists: it says that a house held the agency and NOTHING else — no proprietor, no trade, no street, no roof — because a man who signs for a principal is not thereby a partner in the house he signs for. `refused_holdings` is the same record kept the other way up, for a candidate the printings refute, because the absence of a holding reads exactly like a candidate nobody has judged.

agencies.why: The Howard Fire Insurance Company is a New York company that never stood in this town. It sold fire insurance in Chicago through a LOCAL AGENT, and one standing advertisement — the same setting word for word, only the signature and the number of the verb changing — runs across thirteen months of the corpus: 'THE subscribers having been appointed Agents for the Howard Fire Insurance Company of the city of New-York, for Chicago and the vicinity, will insure property against loss by Fire, on reasonable terms. HUBBARD & CO.' from 1834-07-02, and the identical copy in the SINGULAR over one man, 'THE subscriber having been appointed Agent … E. K. HUBBARD.', from 1835-06-20. Neither the company nor the agency is a house in this town: no printing gives either a street, and nothing here decides whether E. K. Hubbard was a partner in Hubbard & Co., because no printing says so.

holdings.note: Hubbard & Co. held the agency first and advertised it in the PLURAL over the firm's own signature: '[The su]bscribers having been appointed [Ag]ents for the Howard Fire Insurance [Company of] the city of New-York … HUBBARD & CO.' (1834-07-02 c048). The 1834-10-15 c005 and 1835-05-20 c023 printings are the same setting over the copy date 'July 1'. The plural verb and the firm signature are the whole of what makes this the FIRM's holding rather than a partner's, and it is all they make it: the commission and forwarding house gains a line on its card and nothing else — no trade, no street, no roof. 'fire insurance' stands in this record's goods because the notice ran over its signature, which is a fact about the printing and not a second trade.

From 1835-06-20 the identical copy runs in the SINGULAR over one man — 'THE su[bs]criber ha[v]ing been [a]p[poin]t[e]d [agent] for the Howard Fire Insurance [Company] … E. K. [H]UBBARD.', American 1835-06-20 c015, copy-dated June 20, 1835 — and the Democrat reprints it at 1835-07-01 c017, 1835-07-08 c005, 1835-07-29 c011 and 1835-08-05 c008 over the copy date 'July 1'. So on the scene date the agency sits with E. K. Hubbard, and the forwarding house goes on trading under its own name to 1835-08-29. This project never reads a shared surname with different initials as one man, so the holder here is the MAN the signature names and nothing joins him to Hubbard & Co.'s partners, Gurdon S. Hubbard and Henry G. Hubbard. That refusal is exactly what the old `refused_firm_merges` entry was for, and it is what this relation replaces: the two records are not confused, they are joined — by an agency that passed from the firm to one man.

refused_holdings.refused_because: T-0410 was filed reading a THIRD holder off 1835-08-05 c008, where the agency notice is claimed on the Jones, King & Co. business record and that record therefore announced itself 'appointed Agent for the Howard Fire Insurance Company'. The fragment refutes it. Its own reading runs 'July 1, [1835]. [E]. K. [H]UBBARD. — Hardware, Stoves, &c. Th[e] u[n]dersigned have [formed a] connect[ion] in the mercantile business, under the [f]irm o[f] Jones, [King] & [C]o.': two notices on one fragment, as that claim's own notes say, and the fire-insurance card is signed by the man while the hardware notice below it is signed WILLIAM JONES, BYRAM KING, W. B. CLARKE. The claim's own entity list reads 'UCBRARB,' as 'Hubbard, E. K.' with the role 'insurance agent'. Nothing in the setting puts the agency in Jones, King & Co.'s hands; the segmenter put the two advertisements on one line. So there is no handover in the week of 5 August, and this is the fifth printing of the E. K. Hubbard holding above. The claim's `announces_opening` is dropped in the same pass, because it was the agency's sentence read onto the hardware firm's record.

retires.name: E. K. Hubbard, agent for the Howard Fire Insurance Company
retires.because: 'E. K. Hubbard, agent for the Howard Fire Insurance Company' is the agency itself minted as a house, which is the defect T-0410 was filed for. It has no street, no goods and no placement in any of its four printings, because an agency is not a house and none of them gave it one; what it has is a principal and a man holding it, and both of those are now the relation above. Every printing it was compiled from is a witness of the E. K. Hubbard holding, so the register loses one business record and not one reading. The transcriber's em-dashed style 'Howard Fire Insurance Company — E. K. Hubbard, agent at Chicago' that an earlier firm merge collapsed into it is carried onto the retired record, so that judgement outlives the record it was made about.
